what_it_does: Neural network models store billions of numerical weights; 'weight clustering' is a compression technique that groups similar weights together and replaces each group with a single representative value, drastically shrinking the model's storage footprint. A method called Differentiable KMeans (DKM) — where the grouping is learned during training itself rather than applied afterward — achieves the best accuracy after compression, but it requires storing a huge number of intermediate numbers during the learning process (specifically during the backward pass, where the model adjusts itself based on errors). For a seven-billion-parameter model this intermediate memory demand exceeds what any single graphics processing unit (GPU) — the chip used to train models — can hold. eDKM attacks this by finding and eliminating duplicate copies of intermediate data before they are moved to main system memory, and by splitting the remaining data into smaller shards. Together these tricks shrink the per-layer memory cost by 130 times, making it feasible to compress a 7-billion-parameter model to roughly 3 bits per weight on standard GPU hardware.
